chunks: "A flex PCB is a printed circuit built on a flexible polyimide film instead of rigid fibreglass, so it can bend.
Copper traces, usually rolled-annealed copper because it handles bending better, are on the film, protected by a coverlay, a polyimide layer with adhesive, instead of soldermask.
Where you mount parts or connectors you add stiffeners.

The advantages: it's thin and light, it can fold into 3D shapes and fit small spaces, it can flex repeatedly in things like hinges, and it replaces cables and connectors, which removes a failure point and survives vibration well.
That's why it's in phones, cameras, laptops' hinges, hard drives, medical probes and aerospace.

The trade-offs: it costs more, typically several times a rigid board of the same area, it's more delicate to handle and assemble, it has dimensional instability and absorbs moisture, it needs special design rules, like keeping a large bend radius, avoiding vias and sharp corners in the bend area, staggering traces on double-sided boards, and not putting heavy components on unsupported areas.
And it's generally lower-density and lower-layer-count than rigid boards, unless you go to rigid-flex.
So I'd use flex where the mechanical benefits, such as dynamic bending, space or connector elimination, justify the cost."
